newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India UTI chief sees funds inflow rising.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India UTI chief sees funds inflow rising.

text.p: The chairman of India's biggest mutual fund, said on Thursday he was confident of mobilising up to 60 billion rupees ($1.67 billion) in the six months to June 30, and reverse a net outflow of funds.
"We have set a target to raise 50-60 billion rupees," G.P. Gupta, chairman of Unit Trust of India (UTI), told Reuters in an interview. "I'm quite confident."

He expects to garner 10 billion rupees from government-owned companies, which were recently allowed to park their surplus cash in UTI units. It also hopes to attract 5-10 billion rupees of bank funds.

"Moreover, I expect the forthcoming budget to offer incentive for investing in capital markets. The PFs (provident funds) and pension funds may also be allowed to invest in the mutual fund," Gupta said.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to unveil the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.
The UTI chief said it will be able to re-assert itself as the dominant player on the stock markets.
"Our role is getting re-established," he said. "We were unable to play our dominant role because of heavy redemptions. That is now reversed."
Fresh funds raised by UTI in the financial year 1995/96 (July-June) at 65 billion rupees was down 57 percent from the previous year's 150 billion.

The huge redemptions were sparked by withdrawal of tax benefits on corporate investments in UTI's units, the pull-out of funds by state-run firms following a new government order and depressed market conditions.
UTI raised 25 billion rupees in the July-December 1996 period, Gupta said, adding collections normally pick up in the January-March period due to tax-spared investments.
Declining interest rates would spur stock markets, he said.
"We expect the interest rates to decline and the stock market to recover during the course of next year," he said.
Banks' prime lending rates have fallen to 14.5-17 percent from 16.5-19 percent in the past one year.
He said the entry of foreign institutional investors (FIIs) into government securities would help bring down the rates.
Gupta expects corporate profits to improve in fiscal 1997/98 helped by lower interest rates and a pick-up in demand.
"Company results in the financial year ending March (1997) may not be as good as one expected," he said. "The working in the next three months (April-June 1997) will be better."
He said FII inflows during calendar 1997 into Indian stock markets was likely to be about $4-5 billion.
Gupta said he saw more mergers and acquisitions. "With the opening up of the economy there's lot of competition. Industry has to re-organise itself ... to ensure economies of scale."
He said UTI, which holds decisive stakes in most firms, will be guided by safeguarding the value of its holding in taking a decision on hostile takeovers.
"I'll act in a manner to safeguard my investment. I've to protect the value of my share. I have to take a decision on a case to case basis," he said.
UTI plans to give a 40 percent stake to Japan's Nomura Securities in its fully owned broking subsidiary, UTI Securities.
"We may part with 40 percent of our equity... the negotiations have not yet been completed," he said.
Nomura will help UTI Securities to increase its foreign clientele in broking business and placement of securities of Indian firms in international markets, he said.
UTI plans to enter into insurance and is awaiting government guidelines, Gupta added. ($1=35.93 rupees)
